messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the mean under the null) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under null hypothesis? Usually we compute standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null hypothesis. That is indeed the standard error: sigma/sqrt(n). They gave sample_std_dev=1.4, sample_size=40. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) = 1.4 / 6.3249 = approx 0.2215. But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? Actually the null hypothesis test uses the population mean 98.6. But the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null is still sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we use sample sigma as estimate. So answer ~0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? That would be the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((sigma^2/n)+(sigma^2/n))? No.

Let's interpret: "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" might refer to the standard error of the mean difference between sample mean and population mean. That is sqrt((s^2/n)+(sigma^2/N)). But population sigma unknown. So likely they want standard error of sample mean.

Thus answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2215 = -1.805. But they didn't ask for t-statistic.

Thus answer: 0.2215.
